cells.tense: Right now the pull and the motion are the same thing, and you are in it.
cells.act: picture it a year on, turned out well, and keep the picture
cells.ask: Some evening soon, imagine this a year from now, going well, in whatever shape it arrives — and set it somewhere you'll cross it again. No plan needed.
cells.core:
What you're moving toward is pulling you, and the pull comes from something you've lived rather than something you're chasing. That's why the momentum holds through resistance without eating you up: it isn't borrowed, and it isn't a story about you — it's a direction you found by walking. Anyone watching can tell the difference between someone running from something and someone headed somewhere, and you read as the second even on the slow weeks.

There's more in this than you've pictured. Imagine where it's heading a year from now, working out — not a plan, just the image, in whatever shape it arrives — and set it where you'll run into it again. It'll be wrong in the details and roughly right in the direction, which is all an image is for. Nothing needs deciding from it yet. Let it sit there while you keep moving.
cells.sheetLine: You're moving toward something you actually want.
cells.verb: moving toward what you're drawn to

cells.tense: You are already at the next thing before this one has finished, and there will be another next thing.
cells.act: adjust one dial a little, then stop
cells.ask: Choose something you're pushing, ease it back a notch — an adjustment, not a dropped commitment — and then stop touching it.
cells.core:
The drive outruns the destination now. You hit a marker and you're past it before the moment lands, so arrivals feel like staging grounds instead of arrivals. Nothing has gone wrong with the engine; it's just that motion has detached from the thing it was moving toward, and the momentum feels like it belongs to itself. It's still carrying you. It's carrying you past the places you meant to get to.

Choose something you're pushing and ease it back a notch — one small adjustment, not a dropped commitment — then stop touching it. You don't have to recover the destination today. You just have to feel a dial move back toward the middle, once, so you remember the hand is still yours. Small correction, then stop. The push will still be there tomorrow.
cells.sheetLine: You're moving fast enough to miss your own arrivals.
cells.verb: moving toward what you're drawn to

cells.tense: You wanted something and stopped at the edge of it, and you have stayed there since.
cells.act: let the thing end that is already over
cells.ask: Let something end that's already finished — a message sent, a thing packed away, a line drawn — and don't reopen it. That's the whole ask.
cells.core:
There's feeling here and no forward motion. You can picture what you wanted, you can still feel the pull toward it, and your feet haven't moved. That's not laziness and it's not a lack of desire. Something in front of all of it is standing there un-finished — a version of this you're still carrying, a commitment you haven't closed — and it takes the energy the step would have used. What you call stalled is a doorstep with old things stacked on it.

Let something end that's already finished: a message sent, a thing packed away, a line drawn. Don't reopen it. Ending it won't deliver a new direction by Friday. It clears the step, and the pull you already have will start moving you toward something again. Do the one act and stop there.
cells.sheetLine: You're not without desire. You're standing on an unclosed thing.
cells.verb: moving toward what you're drawn to

cells.tense: You are already moving toward what you want while calling it some other name.
cells.act: stop holding up the false thing and watch it come down
cells.ask: Take a hand off something you've been propping up — a plan, a habit, a role — and simply watch what holds without you.
cells.core:
The movement has been going the whole time, and the account you give of it is smaller than the thing itself. You say keeping busy, or getting through, or you point at what you're supposedly waiting for — while you keep heading one direction, session after session, toward something you'd have to lose the old frame to name. You can also be stuck and describe yourself as patient. Either way, the direction is already chosen underneath the language.

Take a hand off something you've been propping up — a plan, a habit, a role — and watch what holds without you. If it stands, you've learned what's actually load-bearing. If it comes down, you've learned it needed to. Either result hands back the effort you were spending on the prop, and that effort is yours. Don't rebuild anything yet.
cells.sheetLine: The direction is already moving. The story hasn't caught up.
cells.verb: moving toward what you're drawn to

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the reader can feel direction coming from their own engagement rather than from pressure — the record supports the capacity, not what the person currently feels. A reasonable reader might say the drive is just anxiety or habit, and the ask still works if that is true, because seeing a year on costs nothing. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any version of 'you were meant to move toward light,' which flatters the card instead of the reader.
